about: The CP5 benchmark: 20 entries = 10 literature theories (the CP3 ratings-fairness theory and 9 from nonprofit finance research), 5 positive controls and 5 negative controls. Each has the plain-language text the Planner gets, one paraphrase and the gold answer its spec is reviewed against. Texts avoid column names (CP4 audit W5). A positive control plants `effect_sd` outcome SDs along the gold exposure, so the gate should call it supported; a negative control replaces the gold exposure with another county's whole exposure history (seeded), so the gate should call it unsupported. The controls are written as ordinary theories so the Planner meets them the way it meets any theory (control recovery includes plan validity). Every gold answer was written before any Planner run.

entries.source: CP3 theory; Tuckman and Chang (1991) on context-blind financial ratios
entries.text: Watchdog-style financial ratings are unfair to nonprofits that work in hard-pressed places: organizations in the most economically distressed quarter of counties get lower scores on the usual 0-10 financial score.
entries.paraphrase: If you score nonprofits the way charity watchdogs do, the ones based in the worst-off local economies come out worse.

entries.source: Tuckman and Chang (1991): equity balance as a vulnerability indicator
entries.text: Nonprofits in poorer counties hold smaller financial reserves relative to their yearly revenue.
entries.paraphrase: The higher a county's poverty rate, the thinner the cushion of net assets its nonprofits keep.

entries.source: Carroll and Stater (2009): revenue diversification and stability
entries.text: In wealthier counties nonprofits spread their revenue over more sources instead of leaning on one.
entries.paraphrase: Higher local household incomes go with less concentrated nonprofit revenue.

entries.source: Greenlee and Trussel (2000): donor base and fundraising cost
entries.text: Where residents earn more, nonprofits pay less to raise each dollar of contributions.
entries.paraphrase: A richer donor base makes fundraising cheaper per dollar raised.

entries.source: Resource dependency: local downturns squeeze nonprofit surpluses (Tuckman and Chang 1991)
entries.text: In counties with high unemployment nonprofits end the year with smaller surpluses relative to revenue.
entries.paraphrase: Local joblessness cuts into the operating margin of the nonprofits there.

entries.source: Financial vulnerability and debt (Tuckman and Chang 1991)
entries.text: Nonprofits in counties where families spend more of their income on housing carry more debt relative to what they own.
entries.paraphrase: A heavy local housing cost burden goes with higher liabilities per dollar of assets.

entries.source: Demand pressure on service providers (resource dependency)
entries.text: Where more people lack health insurance, nonprofits put a larger share of their spending into programs.
entries.paraphrase: A higher uninsured rate in a county pushes its nonprofits to spend more on direct programs.

entries.source: Educated donor bases support reserves (Hager and others on nonprofit capitalization)
entries.text: In counties where more adults finished high school, nonprofits build larger reserves relative to revenue.
entries.paraphrase: Higher high-school completion locally goes with a thicker net-asset cushion for nonprofits.

entries.source: Need and revenue: distressed places grow revenue more slowly
entries.text: Nonprofits in the most economically distressed quarter of counties see slower revenue growth from one year to the next.
entries.paraphrase: Organizations in the hardest-hit local economies grow their revenue more slowly.

entries.text: Where a larger share of residents live in food deserts, nonprofits devote a bigger part of their budget to programs.
entries.paraphrase: More food-desert exposure in a county means more of its nonprofits' spending goes to programs.

entries.text: Nonprofits in higher-poverty counties spend a smaller share of their budget on programs.
entries.paraphrase: The poorer the county, the lower the program share of its nonprofits' spending.

entries.text: In counties with more uninsured people, nonprofits spend a larger share of their budget on management and administration.
entries.paraphrase: A higher uninsured rate goes with a higher administrative share of expenses.

entries.text: Where household incomes are higher, nonprofits spend a smaller share of their budget on fundraising.
entries.paraphrase: Richer counties see a lower fundraising share of nonprofit expenses.

entries.text: In places where more adults report poor or fair health, a larger share of nonprofit spending goes to programs.
entries.paraphrase: Worse community health goes with a bigger program share of nonprofit budgets.

entries.text: Nonprofits in the most economically distressed quarter of counties get lower scores on the usual 0-10 financial score.
entries.paraphrase: Organizations based in the worst-off local economies score lower on the standard financial rating.

entries.text: Nonprofits in more populous counties spend a larger share of their budget on management and administration.
entries.paraphrase: A bigger county population goes with a higher administrative share of nonprofit expenses.

entries.text: Where more adults finished high school, nonprofits spend a larger share of their budget on programs.
entries.paraphrase: Higher high-school completion locally means a bigger program share in nonprofit spending.

entries.text: In counties with more residents in food deserts, nonprofits spend a larger share of their budget on fundraising.
entries.paraphrase: More food-desert exposure goes with a higher fundraising share of nonprofit expenses.

entries.text: In counties with more violent crime, nonprofits spend a smaller share of their budget on programs.
entries.paraphrase: Higher local violent crime goes with a lower program share of nonprofit spending.

entries.text: Nonprofits in counties where more adults report poor or fair health get lower scores on the usual 0-10 financial score.
entries.paraphrase: Worse community health goes with a lower standard financial rating for nonprofits.
